about: I know the early records, so this starts at the 1975 divorce album and walks the peaks after the folk years, ending on the late run where he turned into an old bluesman with a library card.

records.n: Mostly covers of old blues and folk songs; the start of the early run I know.
The protest songs and the first great originals. I know this one.
The bleakest of the topical records. Part of the early run I know.
One night's session where he walks away from protest songs. Part of the early run I know.
Half electric, half acoustic, and the start of the Beat-style word torrents. I know this one.
"Like a Rolling Stone" and "Desolation Row": the full-band peak of the early years. I know this one.
The thin wild mercury sound of Nashville session players and long surreal songs; after the door, this is the record the early run was heading toward.
After the motorcycle crash he came back spare and biblical, three musicians and parables. The quietest left turn in rock.
Straight country with Johnny Cash on one song and a crooner's voice; short and pleasant, and the alt-country line runs through it.
A strange double album of covers and odds that Greil Marcus opened his review of with "What is this shit?". It can wait.
A warm, domestic recovery from Self Portrait; good songs, small stakes.
The soundtrack to Peckinpah's western, mostly instrumental, with "Knockin' on Heaven's Door."
Outtakes the label released after he left for Asylum. Skip it.
His only studio album with the Band; "Forever Young" and some fine playing, but the live record from that tour hits harder.
The 1974 comeback tour with the Band, loud and shouted. Worth hearing once the main path is done.
The door: a breakup record with the depth of a novel, songs told from shifting points of view in time. The best place to meet him after the early years.
The 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, the sound of the old weird America in a basement. Comes after the main path, alongside the Harry Smith anthology.
Scarlet Rivera's violin and long story songs like "Hurricane" and "Isis"; the Rolling Thunder spirit in the studio.
The ragged second leg of the Rolling Thunder Revue.
Big band, backup singers and a muddy mix; good songs buried in the production.
The first born-again gospel record, produced by Jerry Wexler with Mark Knopfler. Fervent and well played, but a detour.
The second gospel album, even more doctrinaire. Can wait.
The end of the gospel trilogy, with "Every Grain of Sand."
The best of the 1980s albums, with Knopfler again; the stronger songs from these sessions ended up on the bootleg series.
Slick mid-80s production on decent songs. Skip it.
Mostly filler, saved only by the eleven-minute "Brownsville Girl" written with Sam Shepard.
His low point: covers and leftovers.
Daniel Lanois's swampy production and a real recovery; the first sign of the late Dylan sound.
Nursery-rhyme songs with a starry cast; a step back after Oh Mercy.
The outtakes, including "Blind Willie McTell"; proof that he left some of his best songs off the records.

records.t: Good as I Been to You
records.n: Solo acoustic folk and blues covers; a reset that led straight to Time Out of Mind.
More solo acoustic covers, darker than Good as I Been to You, with his own liner notes on each song.
The late comeback: Lanois's murky sound and a man walking through a world that's emptied out. Mortality without self-pity.

records.t: The Bootleg Series Vol. 4: Bob Dylan Live 1966, The "Royal Albert Hall" Concert
records.n: The famous "Judas!" show, the electric tour that caused riots. Worth hearing after Blonde on Blonde.
Released on 9/11; jump blues, Tin Pan Alley and stolen lines from Twain and a Japanese gangster memoir. Funny and sly.
The same road-band sound as "Love and Theft", more relaxed; a good one once the path is done.
Accordion and border-town blues; minor but likable.
A sincere Christmas album in his ruined voice. A curiosity.
Long, violent ballads including a fourteen-minute Titanic song; the darkest of the late albums and the next one to hear after the path.
Sinatra standards, sung softly. The first of three standards albums that can wait.
More Sinatra-era standards.
Three discs of standards; for completists.
At 79, a long record of death, history and "Murder Most Foul," seventeen minutes on the Kennedy killing. The late peak.
Re-recordings of older songs from a filmed concert; can wait.

about: From the bleak early folk records to the synth-and-baritone albums of his last decades, ending on the record he made knowing he was dying.

records.n: The debut: "Suzanne," "So Long, Marianne," a poet learning to sing. Back to the start once the path has shown the whole arc.
Even sparser than the debut, with "Bird on the Wire" and "The Partisan." Good, but the next one goes further.
The door: the darkest and most intense of the early records, "Avalanche" and "Famous Blue Raincoat." Guitar, voice, and nothing to hide behind.
A loose live record from the early tours; skip until the studio albums land.

records.t: New Skin for the Old Ceremony
records.n: Bigger arrangements and "Chelsea Hotel #2." The best of the records left off the path.
Produced by Phil Spector, who reportedly held him at gunpoint; the wall of sound swallows him.
Warm, with oud and Mexican mariachi players; a quiet one to come back to.
Has "Hallelujah" and "Dance Me to the End of Love"; the cheap synths that the next record perfected start here.
Cheap keyboards, a voice gone to gravel, and jokes: "First We Take Manhattan," "Tower of Song." The reinvention.
Apocalyptic and funny, written as the Cold War ended and LA burned. The title track is the bleakest dance song you'll hear.

records.t: Cohen Live: Leonard Cohen in Concert
records.n: Live versions from the late 80s and early 90s tours.
Made with Sharon Robinson after five years in a Zen monastery; smooth and hushed, a bit too much so.
Odd and slight, with poems set to music; can wait.
The 2008 comeback tour, which he took on after his manager drained his savings. A generous, warm show.
The start of the late trilogy: spare, wry, and about God and death.
The middle of the late trilogy, bluesier; worth it once the path is done.
Released weeks before he died, with a synagogue choir: "Hineni, I'm ready, my Lord." Where the path ends.
Posthumous, finished by his son Adam from vocal sketches; a coda, not a main record.

about: Murder ballads and gospel rage first, then the long turn toward the grief records, with a stop back at the Birthday Party's noise.

records.n: The Birthday Party's first album under that name; Junkyard is the one that matters.
The Birthday Party at their most feral: scraping guitars, howled Southern Gothic, nothing like rock and roll politeness. Where he came from.
The first Bad Seeds record, still half in the Birthday Party's chaos, with a Leonard Cohen cover.
His Delta blues and Elvis mythology record; interesting but stiff.
Covers album, from Johnny Cash to Gene Pitney; can wait.
Gothic and slow, with "The Carny"; the closest runner-up to Tender Prey from the early years.
"The Mercy Seat," a man in the electric chair; written alongside his Southern Gothic novel. The best of the 1980s albums.
Made in Brazil, sober and string-laden; the first gentle record.
Loud and wordy folk-rock about violence; the producer's thin mix held it back.
A live set from the early 90s tours.
The door: "Red Right Hand" and "Loverman," the Bad Seeds fully formed, menace and love songs on the same record.
Ten songs, sixty-odd killings, including a duet with Kylie Minogue and PJ Harvey on "Henry Lee." Black comedy and folk tradition.
Piano and voice after two breakups, including PJ Harvey; his most naked record. Come back to it at the end if it hasn't been heard already.
Piano ballads with the McGarrigle sisters; good, but the path has stronger records from both sides of it.
The weakest of the Bad Seeds albums apart from the closing fifteen-minute "Babe, I'm on Fire."

records.t: Abattoir Blues / The Lyre of Orpheus
records.n: A double album, one loud gospel record and one quiet one, after Blixa Bargeld left. Ragged and joyous.
Live record from that tour.
Cave and a stripped Bad Seeds playing filthy garage rock; funny midlife-crisis noise.
Lazarus reimagined as a New York burnout; the Grinderman energy brought back to the band. A good next stop after the path.
The second Grinderman record, heavier and stranger.
Warren Ellis's loops replace the band's bluster; quiet, hypnotic, and the start of the late sound.
Finished after his 15-year-old son's death; drones and half-spoken grief. The hardest record on the path.
Ambient hymns about where the dead go: the gentlest answer to Skeleton Tree.
Cave and Ellis alone, made in the 2020 lockdown; dark and electronic.
Ecstatic and choral, the record after the grief trilogy; hear it once the path is done.

about: I know him through the Berlin trilogy, so this starts where Berlin left off, walks the late art records to Blackstar, then goes back for the early classics I haven't heard.

records.n: The music-hall debut, Anthony Newley more than rock. A curiosity.
Also known as Space Oddity. Folk-rock with the hit; can wait.

records.t: The Man Who Sold the World
records.n: Heavy and paranoid, with Mick Ronson. I know this one.
Piano songs about Nietzsche, Warhol and Dylan: "Life on Mars?" and "Quicksand." The best of the early records I haven't heard.

records.t: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars
records.n: The alien rock star concept album, glam at its sharpest. Essential once the late path is done.
Ziggy goes to America, with Mike Garson's avant-garde piano. I know this one.
A covers album of 60s London bands; can wait.
Started as a stage musical of Orwell's 1984. I know this one.
His "plastic soul" record made in Philadelphia. I know this one.
Cocaine and occult funk, the Thin White Duke; the bridge into Berlin and the last big gap after the path.
The first Berlin record with Eno: song fragments on one side, instrumentals on the other. I know this one.
The second Berlin record, with Fripp's guitar on the title track. I know this one.
The last of the trilogy, travelogue art-pop. I know this one.
The door: the Berlin experiments turned into hard, nervy songs, with Fripp's guitar again. The natural next step from the trilogy.
Nile Rodgers and the big hit years; slick and commercial, skip it.
A rushed follow-up to Let's Dance. Skip.
He called it his low point. Skip.
His hard-rock band; noisy and blunt.
The second Tin Machine record.
Wedding-themed and back with Rodgers; the return to form starts here, tentatively.
Nominally a TV soundtrack, really an overlooked art record; Bowie called it a favorite. Worth it after the path.
A murder-mystery concept album with Eno: art-crime in a dystopian 1999, industrial and spoken-word. The Berlin team reunited.
His drum and bass record; dated but energetic.
Soft and reflective, made partly for a video game. Can wait.
With Tony Visconti again, a grown-up record about faith and age.
The rockier companion to Heathen; fine, but Heathen does it better.
The surprise comeback after ten years of silence, its cover a defaced copy of the "Heroes" sleeve. Taut and full of history.
Made while dying with a New York jazz band; released two days before his death. Where everything ends.
Posthumous release of his 2000-01 re-recordings of early songs; for completists.

about: The four Velvet Underground records in order, then Reed's solo peaks, from glam to his grim Berlin to the New York street reporter.

records.n: The door: drones, heroin, "Venus in Furs," and Nico's deadpan; Warhol produced it and few bought it, but it shaped everything after.
Feedback and the seventeen-minute "Sister Ray"; the band at its loudest, with John Cale's viola.
Cale gone, the band turns quiet and tender: "Pale Blue Eyes," "Jesus."
Made for radio: "Sweet Jane" and "Rock & Roll." Reed left before it came out.
Bowie and Mick Ronson produce: "Walk on the Wild Side," "Perfect Day." Glam with a street sense.
Reed's last show with the band, recorded on a cassette by Brigid Berlin from Warhol's circle.
The solo debut, mostly reworked Velvets songs; flat production.
A grim novel in ten songs about a couple falling apart in Berlin; critics hated it, then changed their minds.
Made after Reed left, with Doug Yule alone; not really a Velvet Underground record.
Live hard-rock versions of Velvets songs with heavy guitars.
Live recordings from the 1969 tour; the best live Velvets.
His biggest chart record and one he disowned. Skip.
An hour of feedback that ended his deal and became a sacred text of noise. On the far shelf.
Warm and romantic, the title song is one of his best. The first solo record after the path.
Light and forgettable.
The title song is an eleven-minute street suite with Springsteen reciting a few lines; the rest is uneven.
Reed riffing and insulting critics between songs, like a comedy record.
Free-jazz trumpeter Don Cherry plays on it; odd and late-night.
Domestic and wry; can wait.
With Robert Quine's guitar, a clean, sober record; the best of his 1980s albums apart from New York.
The Quine band again, less striking than The Blue Mask.
Mid-80s and upbeat. Skip.
Unreleased 1968-69 studio recordings, as good as an official album.
His slickest record. Skip.
More outtakes, weaker than VU.
Two guitars, bass, drums and fourteen dispatches about the city in the Reagan years. Reed as reporter.
Reed and John Cale reunite to tell Andy Warhol's life in songs; spare piano, viola and guitar.
A song cycle about two friends dying of cancer; serious and slow.
Happy and loose; can wait.
Long, noisy songs about marriage; uneven.
Reed's Poe album, with Willem Dafoe, Steve Buscemi and Ornette Coleman.
Ambient music for tai chi. A curiosity.
With Metallica, based on Wedekind's Lulu plays; reviled, then grudgingly re-evaluated. On the far shelf.

about: A Rimbaud-obsessed poet fronting a rock band: the four Patti Smith Group records in order, then the comeback after her husband's death.

records.n: The door: "Jesus died for somebody's sins but not mine," Lenny Kaye's garage guitar and John Cale producing. Beat poetry with a rock band.
Louder and messier, a long improvised title track; critics hated it, which is part of its appeal.
"Because the Night" with Springsteen, plus "Rock N Roll Nigger"; her most direct rock record.
Todd Rundgren produces, and she says goodbye before marrying Fred Smith and leaving music for years.
Made with Fred Smith, "People Have the Power"; polished and of its time.
Made after Fred Smith and her brother died; grief, Kurt Cobain and a Tom Verlaine guitar. The comeback.
Beat-influenced, with Ginsberg's "Footnote to Howl" set to music as "Spell"; worth it after the path.
Political and long; uneven.
A two-disc best-of with rarities.
Spiritual and political, closing on a hymn her mother used to sing; solid but not essential.
Covers of Hendrix, Nirvana, Dylan; a curiosity.
Her poem for Robert Mapplethorpe read over Kevin Shields's guitar; a spoken-word record for the Beats side of the list.
The best of her late records, with songs for Amy Winehouse and the Fukushima victims, and a Bulgakov thread.

records.t: The Poet Speaks: Homage to Allen Ginsberg
records.n: Patti Smith with Philip Glass reading and playing Ginsberg.

about: I know After the Gold Rush and Sugar Mountain, so this starts in the dark mid-70s "ditch trilogy" and moves from Crazy Horse's noise to his country side.

records.n: The overproduced solo debut; he disowned the mix.
The first with Crazy Horse: "Down by the River" and "Cowgirl in the Sand," long ragged guitar jams.
Piano, acoustic songs and "Southern Man." I know this one.
His country-rock hit with "Heart of Gold" and "Old Man"; smoother than the rest of the path, but central.
The first of the ditch records, a live album of new songs from a miserable tour.
The door: hungover and paranoid, after the hippie dream curdled. "Ambulance Blues" is nine minutes of Dylan-like despair.
A drunk wake for two friends who died of overdoses; sloppy on purpose, and one of his best.
Crazy Horse back, with "Cortez the Killer"; the next one to hear after the path.
A reunion with Stephen Stills; slight.
A grab bag, but has "Like a Hurricane."
Three-LP career compilation he picked himself, with unreleased songs.
Gentle country-folk; nice, but Harvest covers this ground.
Acoustic side, electric side, both ending in "Hey hey, my my"; his answer to punk.
The Rust Never Sleeps tour live; good once the studio album lands.
Short and divided, half folk, half country; minor.
Crazy Horse on repetitive riffs; minor.
His vocoder and synth record, odd and earnest; the start of his weird Geffen years.

records.c: Neil Young and the Shocking Pinks
records.n: Rockabilly with the Shocking Pinks; a joke on his label.
Straight Nashville country; minor.
Mid-80s drum sounds. Skip.
Crazy Horse in 80s production. Skip.
A horn band record mocking corporate rock sponsorships; fun but minor.
The comeback: "Rockin' in the Free World" in both acoustic and electric forms, bookending a record about America at the end of the 80s.
Crazy Horse at their loudest and most joyous, ten-minute feedback jams; where grunge took notes.
Live with Crazy Horse during the Gulf War, at volume.
A gentle sequel to Harvest twenty years later.
Dark, after Kurt Cobain quoted him in his suicide note; the best of the 90s records left off the path.
Backed by Pearl Jam; loud and loose.
Young improvising on electric guitar while watching Jarmusch's film, with Johnny Depp reading William Blake.
Crazy Horse in a lazy mood; minor.
Quiet acoustic songs; minor.
A soul record with Booker T. & the M.G.'s; minor.
A rock-opera about a small town; long and talky.
Nashville and Harvest-style, written around an aneurysm; warm and mortal.
Written and recorded in two weeks to protest the Iraq War.
A sequel to an unreleased 1977 album, with the eighteen-minute "Ordinary People."

records.t: Sugar Mountain – Live at Canterbury House 1968
records.n: A solo acoustic 1968 show, from before the first album came out. I know this one.
About his electric car. Skip.
Solo electric guitar with Daniel Lanois's echoes; an interesting late one.
Crazy Horse doing old folk songs; fun but minor.
Crazy Horse in long jams again, "Driftin' Back" runs 27 minutes; the best of the late records.
Covers recorded in Jack White's vintage voice-recording booth. A curiosity for the Jack White side of me.
Orchestral and big band; minor.
A protest record against agribusiness, with Promise of the Real; minor.
Sparse and quick; minor.

records.c: Neil Young + Promise of the Real
records.n: With Promise of the Real; minor.
Crazy Horse reunited with Nils Lofgren; solid.
An album shelved in 1975 for Tonight's the Night, finally released; heartbreak songs from the same years as the door.
Crazy Horse in a barn; minor.
Crazy Horse, produced by Rick Rubin; minor.

records.c: Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts
records.n: With his new band the Chrome Hearts; minor.

about: From the confessional folk of Blue into the jazz records she made with the best players of the 70s, ending at her collaboration with Mingus.

records.n: The David Crosby-produced debut; lovely but tentative.
Her own "Both Sides Now" and "Chelsea Morning"; folk-era, can wait.
Laurel Canyon folk with "Big Yellow Taxi" and "Woodstock"; a step back after the path to see where Blue came from.
The door: a confessional record of guitar, piano and dulcimer, written after leaving Graham Nash. Every song is personal.
The bridge from Blue to the jazz years, with Tom Scott's woodwinds; the best of the records left off.
Her biggest hit, with jazz players from the L.A. Express; sophisticated pop with sharp lyrics.
Live with the L.A. Express.
Suburban satire and African drums ("The Jungle Line"); panned at the time, now seen as her most adventurous.
Written on a road trip, built around Jaco Pastorius's fretless bass; restless and jazzy.
A sprawling double album with a sixteen-minute orchestral piece; the most experimental, worth it after Mingus.
Mingus, dying of ALS, asked her to write words for his last melodies; Jaco and Herbie Hancock play. The jazz bridge, made for my side of the list.
Live with Jaco Pastorius, Pat Metheny and Michael Brecker.
A light pop-rock record; minor.
Synthesizers and Thomas Dolby; dated.

records.t: Chalk Mark in a Rain Storm
records.n: More 80s production, with Peter Gabriel and Willie Nelson guesting; minor.
A return to acoustic guitar; quiet and good.
Angry and Grammy-winning, with a Van Gogh self-portrait cover; the best of the later records.
Guitar-synth textures; minor.
Standards with an orchestra, telling a love story; for later.
Her songs re-recorded with orchestra.
Environmental songs after a decade off; minor.

about: From the wild teenage debut to the studio experiments and the long domestic suite of Aerial, with the record built on Joyce after.

records.n: Recorded as a teenager, with "Wuthering Heights" written after a TV adaptation sent her to the novel.
A rushed second album from the same year; minor.
The first she co-produced, with early Fairlight sampling; the best of the records left off.
Her most extreme record: dense sampling, Aboriginal drones, Houdini. Polarising and strange, on the far shelf.
The door: one side of art-pop singles, one side "The Ninth Wave," a suite about someone drifting in the sea at night.
The title song was written to Molly Bloom's soliloquy from Ulysses; she later got the Joyce estate's permission.
Made around a short film; more conventional, and minor.
After twelve years: a double album, the second disc a song cycle about a single summer day. Domestic and luminous.
Long, slow piano songs about snow; a quiet late record to finish on.
Re-recordings of songs from The Sensual World and The Red Shoes, including the Joyce lyric she was first refused; for later.
Her 2014 return to live performance, with The Ninth Wave staged in full.

about: From the raw trio records to the war songs of Let England Shake and the dialect poems of her latest, with a look back at the debut.

records.n: The trio debut, blunt and sharp; heard after the path, it shows where Rid of Me came from.
The door: Steve Albini's live, violent recording, vicious and funny, songs about desire and revenge.
Home demos of Rid of Me songs plus unused ones; for after the album.
Blues and gothic, with the band behind her and organ; theatrical, closer to Nick Cave.
Experimental record with John Parish; worth it after the path.
Short stories set to electronics; underrated but minor.

records.t: Stories from the City, Stories from the Sea
records.n: New York and Dorset, with Thom Yorke dueting on "This Mess We're In"; her most accessible.
Lo-fi and played almost all by herself; minor.
Radio sessions across the years.
Piano and a high, ghostly voice; a hushed Victorian record that pairs well with Ghosteen.

records.t: A Woman a Man Walked By
records.n: The second John Parish record; noisier.
War songs from Gallipoli to Afghanistan, with autoharp; poetry about history, not slogans.
Recorded in public at Somerset House, about Kosovo, Afghanistan and Washington D.C.; uneven but interesting.
Incidental music for the Ivo van Hove stage production.

records.t: I Inside the Old Year Dying
records.n: Songs from her book-length dialect poem Orlam, set in rural Dorset; strange and lovely.

about: From the nervous art-school debut to the Afro-funk of Remain in Light and the concert film, with the Byrne and Eno collage that came out of it.

records.n: The nervy debut, "Psycho Killer" and minimal guitar; where they started.

records.t: More Songs About Buildings and Food
records.n: The first Eno production; tighter and funkier. The next record to hear after the path.
Paranoid and darker, "Life During Wartime" and the Hugo Ball poem "I Zimbra."
The door: Afrobeat and Fela-inspired polyrhythms, loops and Byrne's anxious sermons. With Eno.

records.t: My Life in the Bush of Ghosts
records.n: Byrne and Eno's sampling record, found voices over funk loops; the same lab as Remain in Light.

records.t: The Name of This Band Is Talking Heads
records.n: Live record from 1977 to 1981, with the big band; worth hearing after the studio albums.
"Burning Down the House" and "This Must Be the Place"; the funk band at its most joyful.
The concert film soundtrack, the band built up one player at a time. The live culmination.
Short, sunny pop songs; minor.
Songs from Byrne's film about a Texas town; slight.
Recorded in Paris with African players; a fitting last record, minor.

about: I've tried the ambient records; this path is his song albums, the strange art-pop that sits between Bowie's Low and Talking Heads.

records.n: His first band, glam with Eno on synths and tapes.
The second Roxy Music record, Eno's last with them.
Long loops with Robert Fripp's guitar; ambient before ambient.
The first solo song record: glam, noise, and words chosen for their sound.
A concept album about Chinese revolutionary opera and espionage; catchy and weird.
The door: half instrumentals, half songs, made with Oblique Strategies cards; the bridge between the songs and ambient.
An early ambient record, conceived while he was laid up after an accident; part of the ambient side, not this path.
The second Fripp and Eno record, gentler.
The last of the song records, split between nervy rock and hushed pastoral songs.
With the German duo Cluster; for after the path.
Tape loops for an airport terminal. I know this one.
Short cues for imaginary films; ambient.
With Harold Budd's piano.
Jon Hassell's processed trumpet; a world-music-meets-ambient experiment.

records.t: My Life in the Bush of Ghosts
records.n: With David Byrne; on the Talking Heads path.
Darker ambient landscapes; the best of the ambient series.
With Daniel Lanois and Roger Eno for a moon-landing documentary; ambient.
Song album with John Cale; wry and warm, his first singing in years.
His first solo vocal album in decades; quieter and melancholic.

records.t: Everything That Happens Will Happen Today
records.n: With David Byrne, "electronic gospel"; the late song record to finish on.

records.t: Small Craft on a Milk Sea
records.c: Brian Eno, Jon Hopkins & Leo Abrahams
records.n: With Leo Abrahams and Jon Hopkins; instrumental soundscapes.
Settings of Rick Holland's poems; worth it for the poetry side of the list.
Songs about the climate crisis in his own voice; slow and grave.

about: I know them all; this is a re-listen order that starts at my two favorites and walks forward through the studio years, then goes back to hear where the songwriting came from.

records.n: The debut, mostly cut in one day; the energy is great, but half of it is covers.
More of the debut's formula, with Motown and girl-group covers.
Then go back: the first album of all Lennon-McCartney songs, and George's twelve-string chime that the Byrds took whole.
The tired one, made between tours; the country and Carl Perkins side of the band, worth a later visit.
The door, again: the first record made as an album, with folk-rock guitars, a sitar on "Norwegian Wood" and lyrics that turn inward.
The bridge into Rubber Soul: "Yesterday," "You've Got to Hide Your Love Away" and the Dylan influence arriving.
The other favorite, straight after: tape loops, backwards guitar and "Tomorrow Never Knows," the point where the studio becomes the instrument.

records.t: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
records.n: The concept-album idea Revolver made possible; hear it right after to see how much is costume and how much is new.
The 1967 singles collected with the film songs: "Strawberry Fields Forever," "Penny Lane," "I Am the Walrus." The psychedelic peak lives here as much as on Pepper.
The White Album: four songwriters pulling apart, from "Helter Skelter" to "Revolution 9." The sprawl is the point.
The last record they made together, with the side-two medley as a deliberate farewell.
Four new songs and a side of George Martin's film score.
Recorded before Abbey Road and released after the breakup; the rooftop songs are better in the film.
The non-album singles and B-sides, including "Rain" and "Hey Jude"; worth having but not a record to study.

about: Ray Davies at his most English and most literary, from the 1966 turn to character songs through the early-1970s Americana record.

records.n: The debut, built around "You Really Got Me"; the riff is history, the rest is filler and covers.
Rushed out between tours; "Tired of Waiting for You" is the one to keep.
The garage-rock band starting to turn into Ray Davies's band; "Where Have All the Good Times Gone" points ahead.
Back to where the observing started: "Sunny Afternoon" and satire of the rich and the bored.
The year before: "Waterloo Sunset," "Two Sisters," and Dave Davies's "Death of a Clown." Character songs in three minutes.
A live record mostly of screaming fans.

records.t: The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society
records.n: The door: a gentle, funny concept record about a vanishing English village, which sold almost nothing and became the one everyone treasures.

records.t: Arthur (Or the Decline and Fall of the British Empire)
records.n: Written for a TV play that was never made: one family's life from Victoria to emigration to Australia, with louder guitars.

records.t: Lola Versus Powerman and the Moneygoround, Part One
records.n: The music business as a villain, with "Lola" and "Apeman" in the middle of it.
North London working-class life set to American country and music hall; the most alt-country thing in the British Invasion.
Half studio, half live; "Celluloid Heroes" is the song to know.
The start of the overreaching rock-theater period.
More of the Preservation story, for those already invested in it.

records.t: The Kinks Present a Soap Opera
records.n: Another theatrical concept album; thin songs.

records.t: The Kinks Present Schoolboys in Disgrace
records.n: The last of the theater records, a prequel to Preservation.
The start of the arena-rock run on Arista.
Arena-era, with a good title song.
Big, loud and American; a hit, but slicker than the 1960s work.
The arena-era band live.

records.t: Give the People What They Want
records.n: Arena rock with Ray's sharper lyrics.
Has "Come Dancing"; otherwise for completists.
Late-period; the band was coming apart.
Late-period, mostly forgotten.
Late-period, mostly forgotten.
The last studio album.

about: The 1968 to 1972 run, when the Stones went back to blues and country and made four records in a row that hold up; then a few side doors around it.

records.n: The debut, almost all blues and R&B covers.
More covers; still a blues band learning.
Mostly covers; the US version has "Satisfaction" on it.
The first album of all Jagger-Richards songs, with Brian Jones on marimba and dulcimer.
Their most English pop record, a near-miss that has its fans.
The psychedelic detour; "2000 Light Years from Home" is worth one listen.
Back to the start of the run: acoustic blues, "Sympathy for the Devil" and "Street Fighting Man."
"Gimme Shelter" to "You Can't Always Get What You Want"; the end of the 1960s as a record.
The 1969 tour live, Mick Taylor and Keith trading guitars; the band at its rawest.
Mick Taylor's guitar, "Wild Horses," "Sister Morphine" and the long jam of "Can't You Hear Me Knocking."
The singles that never made the UK albums: "Satisfaction," "Jumpin' Jack Flash," "Honky Tonk Women."
The door: a murky, sprawling double album recorded in a basement in France, blues and gospel and country under the mud.
The hangover after Exile; "Angie" and a lot of drift.
Mick Taylor's last; uneven.
Guitarist auditions on tape; "Memory Motel" and "Fool to Cry."
The late return: punk-sharp, with "Beast of Burden" and "Shattered."
Disco and leftovers.
Assembled from outtakes; has "Start Me Up" and a soft second side.
The 1980s sheen the list steers away from.
Made while Mick and Keith weren't speaking.
The stadium comeback.
Competent and long.
Late-period, mostly forgotten.
Late-period, louder than it needs to be.
An album of blues covers cut in three days; a fun return to where they started.
The big-budget late album, with guests.
The newest; not needed to understand the band.

about: Two doors, Syd Barrett's psychedelic debut and Roger Waters's lament for him, then the Waters concept records of the 1970s.

records.t: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn
records.n: The first door: Syd Barrett's only full album with the band, nursery rhymes and gnomes against the space-rock of "Interstellar Overdrive."
The transition: Syd fading out, David Gilmour coming in; the title track is the reason to hear it.
A film score; some pretty folk songs and a lot of mood.
Half live, half solo experiments; the live half is the good half.
Syd's first solo record, fragile and broken, produced in part by Gilmour and Waters.
Syd's second and last solo album.
The orchestral side-long suite; the band disowned it later.
After the path: the side-long "Echoes" is where the Dark Side sound began.
Another film score, recorded quickly between bigger records.

records.t: The Dark Side of the Moon
records.n: Back two years: madness, money and time, with the band's studio craft at its peak.
The second door: eight years on, the band's song for Syd, and a sour one about the music industry.
Orwell's farm, rewritten for 1970s Britain: dogs, pigs and sheep, in long angry songs.
Waters's double-album rock opera about isolation; the end of the classic band.
Essentially a Waters solo record about the Falklands War; bitter and thin.
Gilmour's Floyd without Waters, with a 1980s sheen.
Gilmour's Floyd, smoother.
Ambient leftovers from the Division Bell sessions.

about: Zappa as satirist and composer: the jazz-rock door, the Mothers' early lampoons, the 1970s hits and the Joe's Garage parable, then the chamber music he cared about most.

records.n: Back to the start: a double debut that mocks hippies and squares alike and ends in a long tape-collage freak-out.
The second Mothers record, two side-long suites; good, but Money does the same thing better.

records.t: We're Only in It for the Money
records.n: A parody of Sgt. Pepper and the Summer of Love, chopped up with tape edits; satire as dense as Pynchon.
An orchestral and tape-collage piece, the companion to Money; for after the path.
A loving parody of doo-wop.
The door: mostly instrumental jazz-rock, with Captain Beefheart singing on "Willie the Pimp" and Zappa's guitar out front.
Back to the Mothers for the composer: tape music, Varèse-like percussion and a soundtrack to a film that never got made.
Leftovers from the original Mothers, with some fine instrumentals.
More of the original Mothers' archive, noisier.
A transition record between bands.
The Flo & Eddie band live; mostly groupie comedy.
Soundtrack to his film; a mess with some orchestral moments.
More of the Flo & Eddie band live.
Big-band jazz-rock recorded while he recovered from being pushed off a stage.
The big-band follow-up to Waka/Jawaka; worth it if Hot Rats lands.
The sibling to Apostrophe, cruder and funnier.
The 1970s Zappa most people know: an Eskimo saga and "Cosmik Debris," tight and funny.
The 1973 band live, maybe his best live band.
The best of the 1970s bands, with George Duke and Ruth Underwood; "Inca Roads" is the showpiece.

records.c: Frank Zappa, Captain Beefheart and the Mothers of Invention
records.n: A live reunion with Captain Beefheart.
A leaner rock record.
A live record with a horn section and "The Black Page."
Released from the vault during a label fight.
A rock opera about a country that bans music; a central scrutinizer narrates, Kafka by way of a garage band.
The story's second half, released two months later, ending in "Watermelon in Easter Hay," his best guitar solo.
More vault material from the same label fight.
His biggest seller, crude comedy rock.
Orchestral pieces from 1975.
Live, mostly punk-era parody.
Guitar solos edited from live shows, for guitar people.
Satire of the early 1980s, religion and fashion; sharp but dated.

records.t: Ship Arriving Too Late to Save a Drowning Witch
records.n: Has "Valley Girl," his only hit single.
Uneven early-1980s record.
His chamber music conducted by Pierre Boulez; a preview of The Yellow Shark.
Mid-1980s rock record.
A broadway satire that offends nearly everyone; for after the path.

records.t: Frank Zappa Meets the Mothers of Prevention
records.n: Includes his response to the record-labeling hearings in Washington.
Almost all Synclavier; won a Grammy.
Live political satire from the 1988 tour.

records.t: You Can't Do That on Stage Anymore, Vol. 1
records.n: The first of six volumes of live recordings from every era; a library, not a record.
Instrumentals from the 1988 tour.
The last record of his lifetime: his chamber music played by Ensemble Modern, the serious composer he always said he was.

about: Prince as a one-man band and studio maximalist, from the new-wave funk of Dirty Mind to the double-album peak of Sign o' the Times.

records.n: The debut, made alone at nineteen; slick R&B.
The second, with "I Wanna Be Your Lover."
Back to the start of his real voice: cheap synths, punk speed, home-recorded.
Between Dirty Mind and 1999; the title song is the reason.
Long synth-funk grooves; the Minneapolis sound, at full length.
The soundtrack and the blockbuster; the guitar in "Purple Rain" and the bare "When Doves Cry."

records.t: Around the World in a Day
records.n: The psychedelic follow-up to Purple Rain; a gentler Parade.
After the path: a strange, European-flavored record from his film Under the Cherry Moon, with "Kiss."
The door: a double album that covers funk, psychedelia, gospel and the news in its title song, played mostly by Prince alone.
A sequenced, single-track gospel-funk record; pleasant but slight.
Soundtrack to the Tim Burton film.
Soundtrack to his flop sequel to Purple Rain.

records.c: Prince and the New Power Generation
records.n: Polished, commercial 1990s R&B.

records.c: Prince and the New Power Generation
records.n: Its title is a glyph; long and uneven.
From the years he fought Warner Bros.
Withdrawn in 1987 and released officially in 1994; raw funk, for after the path.
The best of his 1990s records, with "The Most Beautiful Girl in the World."
Delivered to finish his Warner contract.
Three CDs to celebrate his freedom; too long.
Vault material sold by mail order.
A late-1990s pop attempt.
Jazz-funk concept record about his faith.
Just Prince at a piano, quiet and good.
The return to form most critics named at the time.
Mid-2000s, light.
Given away free with a newspaper.
A double set sold through Target.
Given away free with newspapers in Europe.
His return to Warner Bros.
A guitar-rock record with his band 3rdEyeGirl.
Late electronic funk.
His last album in his lifetime.
A posthumous cassette of him alone at the piano in 1983; a short, intimate extra.

about: Springsteen as a Steinbeck novelist with a guitar: starting from the stark home recordings, then the big records they grew out of and the folk records that came after.

records.t: The Wild, the Innocent & the E Street Shuffle
records.n: Back to the beginning: long, jazzy street operas, closer to Van Morrison than to arena rock.
The wordy, Dylan-styled debut.
The other side of him: Spector-sized rock about escaping a dead-end town.

records.t: Darkness on the Edge of Town
records.n: The town didn't let go: harder, tighter songs about work and family.
A double album that mixes bar-band rock with the bleak songs that point to Nebraska.
The door: songs about killers and losers, recorded alone on a four-track cassette in his bedroom and released as is.
The huge one; the title song is a protest song people mistake for a cheer, but the production is the slick 1980s sound.
Three discs of the E Street Band live; for after the studio records.
Quiet songs about a failing marriage, made mostly alone; the adult record after Born in the U.S.A.
Released the same day as Lucky Town; the weaker of the two.
The better of the 1992 pair, but both can wait.
Nebraska's sequel, built on Steinbeck and on migrant lives along the border; Steinbeck's ghost, literally.
Four discs of outtakes; a sign of how much he left off the albums.
His response to September 11.
A quieter acoustic record in the Tom Joad line; the first one to hear after the path.

records.t: We Shall Overcome: The Seeger Sessions
records.n: Pete Seeger songs played by a loose folk big band.
Rock record about the Iraq War years.
Late-period, lighter.
Angry songs about the financial crash.
Covers and reworked outtakes.
Orchestral, 1970s-California pop.
The E Street Band live in the studio.
A soul covers album.

about: Cash in prisons and at the end of his life, then back to the Sun records and the 1960s concept albums where his storytelling started.

records.t: Johnny Cash with His Hot and Blue Guitar!
records.n: Now go back to Sun: the boom-chicka-boom sound and the first "Folsom Prison Blues."
His first Columbia album; fine, not essential.
An early concept record about death and the land.
A spoken-word railroad tour of America; Cash as a Steinbeck narrator.
Work songs, a cousin of Ride This Train; "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer."

records.t: Bitter Tears: Ballads of the American Indian
records.n: A protest record about Native Americans that radio wouldn't play; "The Ballad of Ira Hayes."
Dylan covers and the harmonica-led title track.

records.t: Johnny Cash Sings the Ballads of the True West
records.n: A double album of cowboy songs and narrations; long but rewarding later.
The door: a show for the inmates, with "Folsom Prison Blues" and the crowd cheering the murder line.
The follow-up prison show, looser and angrier; "A Boy Named Sue" and "San Quentin" played twice in a row.
Made at the peak of his TV fame; uneven.
The title song is his creed; the rest is weaker.

records.c: Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Johnny Cash & Kris Kristofferson
records.n: The supergroup with Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson and Kris Kristofferson.
Rick Rubin sits him in a living room with a guitar; murder ballads and hymns, sparse as Nebraska.
Tom Petty's band behind him on Soundgarden, Beck and old country songs.
Strong, but the path already has the best of the Rubin records.

records.t: American IV: The Man Comes Around
records.n: The last record of his lifetime, with "Hurt" and the apocalyptic title song.
Five discs of Rubin-session outtakes.
Posthumous, finished from his last sessions; very frail.
The last of the posthumous Rubin records.

about: The songwriter's songwriter: a live solo set to start, then the early studio records under the strings and overdubs.

records.t: For the Sake of the Song
records.n: The debut, smothered in production he later disliked; the self-titled record redoes most of it.
The self-titled third album, re-recordings of earlier songs in plainer arrangements; "Waitin' Around to Die" and "For the Sake of the Song."
Earlier the same year: "Kathleen" and "Tecumseh Valley," with heavier orchestral production.
A plainer, darker record; "To Live Is to Fly."
A good record with blues covers; the first to hear after the path.

records.t: The Late Great Townes Van Zandt
records.n: "Pancho and Lefty" and "If I Needed You"; the title was a joke that became true.

records.t: Live at the Old Quarter, Houston, Texas
records.n: The door: recorded in a small Houston bar in 1973, just Townes and a guitar, the songs without any studio dressing.
After a long gap: a fuller country band, and the title song.
His first studio album in nine years, plainly recorded.
A live record from 1978, a second Old Quarter in tone.
Songs recorded in 1972 and 1973 and shelved for twenty years.
His last studio album, made in Ireland.

about: Whispered double-tracked songs, from the home-recorded records to the Beatles-sized studio albums.

records.n: The four-track debut, recorded without plans to release it.
The record before: darker and barer, nearly all acoustic guitar and voice.
The last album by his rock band Heatmiser, where his songs were already taking over.
The door: home-recorded mostly by himself, quiet and precise, with "Between the Bars" and "Say Yes."
The first studio album: the same songwriting with piano, strings and Beatles harmonies.
Recorded partly at Abbey Road; the biggest-sounding of his records.

records.t: From a Basement on the Hill
records.n: Finished after his death; rougher and noisier, a record he never got to complete.
Two discs of outtakes from 1994 to 1997; good, but after the albums.

about: I know Illinois; this path starts there and walks through the states, the banjo record, the electronic turn and the grief records.

records.n: The rough debut; more interesting than good.
An electronic album about the Chinese zodiac; the seeds of Adz.
The first of the states records; banjo, brass and Detroit, the template for Illinois.
Quiet banjo songs about faith, between the two states records.
The door, already open: I know this one.
Outtakes from Illinois; for after the path.
Five EPs of home-recorded Christmas songs.
Orchestral suite about a Brooklyn expressway, with a film.
The electronic turn: glitchy and huge, inspired by the outsider artist Royal Robertson.
An hour-long EP released just before Adz.
A second Christmas box.
Spare songs about his mother's death; the best of him after Illinois.

records.c: Sufjan Stevens, Bryce Dessner, Nico Muhly & James McAlister
records.n: A song cycle on the planets, with trombones and electronics.
The full electronic album, angry about America; if Adz lands, this comes next.
New-age synth instrumentals with his stepfather.
Songs written while watching films, with Angelo De Augustine.
Five volumes of ambient instrumentals about grief.
Gentle songs, with the choirs and banjos of Illinois back in them.

about: Matt Berninger's baritone over brothers Aaron and Bryce Dessner's guitars and arrangements: anxious, literate rock about adult life.

records.n: The debut; country-tinged, not yet their sound.
The second; the voice is there, the band isn't yet.
An EP that bridges to Alligator.
The record before: rougher and angrier, with "Mr. November" and "Abel."
The door: steady drums, horns and piano, songs about middle-class unease.
Boxer outtakes and live tracks.
Bigger and denser, with "Bloodbuzz Ohio" and "Afraid of Everyone."
Quieter, looser, the most melodic of their records.
Electronics creep in, around a marriage coming apart.
Built around guest female singers and a short film; long.
Late, sparse and depressed, with Phoebe Bridgers and Sufjan Stevens as guests.
The surprise companion to Frankenstein, looser.
A live record from their 2024 show in Rome; for after the studio albums.

about: Start with the record where the alt-country band came apart into something stranger, then go back and watch Jeff Tweedy get there.

records.n: Tweedy's first band with Jay Farrar; the record that named a whole alt-country movement.
Uncle Tupelo's last and best album, Farrar and Tweedy trading songs right before the split that produced Son Volt and Wilco.
The straight alt-country debut, made right after the Uncle Tupelo split; pleasant, and the least Wilco-sounding record here.
A double album that breaks out of country-rock into Stones swagger, feedback and drunk ballads; the first sign of the band's range.
Unrecorded Woody Guthrie lyrics set to new music, sung half by Bragg and half by Tweedy; a direct line back to the Dust Bowl.
Bright Beach Boys arrangements over some of Tweedy's darkest lyrics; it's on the list on its own too.
More from the same sessions; good, but the first volume has the best songs.
Songs about radio static and lost signals, wrapped in noise and found sound; the record that got them dropped by their label and then made their name.
Nels Cline-style guitar freakouts before Nels Cline joined, plus a fifteen-minute drone; the end of the experimental run.
A strong live set from the first lineup with Nels Cline; worth it once the studio records are in.
The settled, warm, guitar-solo record that followed the chaos; quieter, and it shows what the new band could do as players.
A well-made, comfortable record; nothing here that the earlier albums don't do better.
Opens with a seven-minute noise-pop track and closes with a twelve-minute ballad; the middle is ordinary.
A short, scrappy surprise release; fun, slight.
Small acoustic songs about childhood; a minor companion to Tweedy's solo work.
Hushed and drum-heavy; a mood record more than a destination.
A double album of country songs recorded live in the room, with the band finally embracing the label they'd spent decades dodging.
Produced by Cate Le Bon, with a cooler, stranger sheen; a reasonable late record to hear after the rest.

about: Four records that drift from a cabin in the Wisconsin woods into glitchy, processed collage; the path follows that drift in order.

records.n: Justin Vernon alone in a hunting cabin, falsetto and acoustic guitar; self-released in 2007, widely issued in 2008.
Four-song EP; the title track and the Auto-Tuned 'Woods' point toward everything that came next.
A full band, horns and pedal steel, each song named for a place; the cabin opened up into a landscape.
Chopped-up vocals, saxophone choirs and broken electronics; the hardest and most interesting record of the three.
Ties the earlier sounds together in a warmer, communal way; the natural last stop.
Three-song EP of stripped, sad songs that closes out the old era.
A turn toward glossy, contented soft-rock and R&B; easy to leave for later.

about: Only three studio albums, so the path covers all of them, then the live record and Beth Gibbons on her own.

records.n: Scratched vinyl, spy-film strings and Beth Gibbons sounding heartbroken over slow breakbeats; the trip-hop record everyone knows.
A short promotional compilation of mixes and B-sides; not needed.
Colder and more abrasive than the debut, built from their own recordings pressed to vinyl and sampled back.
The songs played with a thirty-piece orchestra in New York; heavier and more dramatic than the studio versions.
Gibbons with Talk Talk's bassist, making a smoky 1960s folk-jazz record; it's on the list on its own too.
Eleven years later: krautrock pulses, a machine-gun drum loop and a ukulele; nothing like trip-hop.
Gibbons' first true solo album, about middle age and loss, with hand percussion and strings; a quiet ending.

about: The Bristol collective that more or less invented trip-hop; start with the darkest record, then go back to the start.

records.n: Soul samples, dub bass and low-key raps; where the Bristol sound began.
Softer and more spacious, with Tracey Thorn singing the title track; the bridge between the first record and Mezzanine.
Tricky's solo debut after leaving the group, murkier and more paranoid; it's on the list on its own too.
Mad Professor's dub remix of Protection; good if the bass is what pulls you in.
Heavy guitars, slow menace and Elizabeth Fraser on 'Teardrop'; the darkest and most complete of their records.
A singles box; the albums cover it.
Mostly Robert Del Naja alone, cold and electronic, with Sinéad O'Connor guesting; less loved, but it shows where the group went.
Instrumental score for a Jet Li film; background music.
Best-of; skip it.
A return to guests and grooves, with Damon Albarn and Hope Sandoval; it's on the list on its own too.
Four-track EP with Tricky back on one song; a postscript.

about: Start with the record where strings and beats finally fused, then walk through the run from Debut to Medúlla, and on to the breakup album.

records.n: Her Icelandic post-punk band; fun and jagged, the background to everything after.
Icelandic jazz standards with a piano trio; a charming detour.
House beats, harps and show tunes; the first solo record, bright and curious.
Wilder and more scattered, swinging from big band to industrial noise; she's trying everything at once.
Icelandic strings and volcanic, crunching beats; the most unified record she made and the one where it all clicks.
Songs from Dancer in the Dark, built from factory and train sounds; worth hearing with the film.
Whispered, music-box intimacy made from micro-beats, harps and choirs; a winter record.
Made almost entirely from voices: throat singers, beatboxers, choirs; it's on the list on its own too.
Score for Matthew Barney's film; for completists.
Brass and Timbaland beats; the loudest and least focused album.
Released as a set of apps about nature and music theory; the concept is more interesting than the songs.
A chronological account of a breakup, strings and stark beats; the most direct record she has made.
Flutes and birdsong after the breakup album; lush and long.
Bass clarinets, gabber beats and grief for her mother, framed around mushrooms; a strong late record.

about: Four albums that read like linked novels about Compton, fame and conscience; then the side records that fill in the story.

records.n: The early EP under his real name; a talented rapper still finding the voice.
The last mixtape before the albums; for completists.
The independent debut, about kids born into the Reagan and crack era; a sketchbook for what came next.
A day in teenage Compton told as a film, skits and voicemails from his parents included; the story that makes everything else click.
Free jazz, funk and spoken word with Kamasi Washington and Thundercat; a long poem on race and success.
Jazz-heavy leftovers from the Butterfly sessions; rough and alive.
Tighter and harder, built on the question of wickedness or weakness; it won a Pulitzer.
A curated soundtrack with many guests; a side project.
A double album of therapy sessions and family trauma; uncomfortable and deliberate.
A short, West Coast party record that came out of a feud; fun, but not part of the main arc.

about: Beck alternates between collage records and sad acoustic ones; the path takes both strands, starting with the collage that made his name.

records.n: A cassette of lo-fi noise and folk; for completists.
'Loser' and its slacker folk-hop neighbors, made on a four-track; the first draft of Odelay.
Bare acoustic folk and blues cut for the K label in Olympia; the root of the sad-Beck records.
Scrappy home recordings, country to noise; fun in pieces.
Hip-hop beats, slide guitar and samples from everywhere, made with the Dust Brothers; the collage at its best.
A quick, unpolished album of melancholy folk and bossa nova, cut in two weeks.
A deliberately ridiculous Prince-style funk record; the joke is the point, and it's a good one.
Breakup songs with Nigel Godrich and lush strings, some lifted from Gainsbourg's Melody Nelson, which is on the list too.
A return to the Odelay sound with the Dust Brothers; competent, familiar.
Remixes of Guero; skip.
Long, loose and produced by Godrich; a few good songs in a sprawl.
Short psych-pop with Danger Mouse; fine.
A companion to Sea Change, sunlit rather than broken; same players, same strings.
Glossy, radio-ready pop; the furthest he gets from the scrappy records.
Moody synth-pop with Pharrell Williams; skip for now.
The newest record, said to return to the Sea Change and Morning Phase mode; one to hear after the path.

about: Desert-rock riffs played with machine precision; start with the classic, then trace Josh Homme backward and forward.

records.n: Josh Homme's earlier band at its peak, fuzzed-out desert jams; where the sound came from.
The debut, hypnotic repeated riffs and Homme's 'robot rock' idea in its pure form.
Shorter, stranger songs, with Mark Lanegan and Rob Halford guesting; a druggy, funny record.
A drive through the desert flipping between hellish radio stations, with Dave Grohl on drums and Lanegan singing; the band's best.
Darker and murkier after Nick Oliveri left; good in parts.

records.t: Over the Years and Through the Woods
records.n: Live film and album; for fans.
Clanky and abrasive; a cult favorite but uneven.
Written after Homme nearly died, slower and more piano-led, with Elton John and Trent Reznor along the way; their most personal record.
Produced by Mark Ronson, with a dance-rock gloss; skip for now.
A raw, bitter record written through divorce and illness; worth it after the path.

about: Two guys from Akron playing Junior Kimbrough-style hill-country blues in a basement, and then getting famous; the path stays near the basement.

records.n: The debut, raw two-piece blues covers and originals; Thickfreakness does it better.
Recorded in one fourteen-hour session in Patrick Carney's basement; fuzz, slide and nothing else.
Made in an abandoned tire factory in Akron; the best balance of raw blues and real songs.

records.t: Chulahoma: The Songs of Junior Kimbrough
records.n: A six-song EP of covers of the Mississippi bluesman they learned from; the clearest look at the source.
Their first major-label album, still self-recorded; more of the same, a bit flatter.
Danger Mouse produces, adding flutes and organ; it's on the list on its own too.
The band backing rappers including Mos Def and RZA; an odd, fun side project.
Muscle Shoals soul and falsetto, the record that made them stars; still rough enough to fit.
Glam and rockabilly singles; the slick, arena turn.
Psychedelic and polished; skip.
A guitar-rock reset; fine, forgettable.
Hill-country blues covers cut live with Kimbrough's and R.L. Burnside's old sidemen; a full circle back to Chulahoma.
Short and loose with guests like Billy Gibbons; minor.
Pop collaborations with Beck and Noel Gallagher; the commercial end.
More polished rock; skip.
A covers album of Earl Hooker, R.L. Burnside and Junior Kimbrough songs; worth checking after Delta Kream.

about: A ruined baritone that runs from Seattle grunge to cracked folk and murky electronic blues; start with the noir record, then the folk ones.

records.n: Screaming Trees' psychedelic garage years; for later.
His first solo record, sparse acoustic blues with Kurt Cobain guesting on a Lead Belly song.
Screaming Trees' major-label debut, produced with Chris Cornell; a step toward Sweet Oblivion.
Screaming Trees' big record, heavy psychedelic grunge with Lanegan at full roar.
Hushed, lonely folk-blues made over several hard years; the voice at its most bruised.
Screaming Trees' last album, more polished and Eastern-tinged; a good goodbye.
Quiet, late-night folk in the same vein as Whiskey; minor but lovely.
A covers record of soul, blues and country songs; a short, warm detour.
Spare, steady acoustic songs; the best of the folk records.
Drum machines, distorted blues and guests from PJ Harvey to Josh Homme; noir with menace, and the easiest way in.
Lanegan's baritone against Isobel Campbell's whisper, a Nancy and Lee record for the gutter.

records.t: It's Not How Far You Fall, It's the Way You Land
records.n: Gospel-tinged electronic soul with Soulsavers; worth it if Bubblegum hooks you.
Lanegan and Greg Dulli as the Gutter Twins; dark, dramatic rock.
The second record with Isobel Campbell; more of the first.
The third Campbell record; the weakest.
Krautrock pulses and synths under his blues; the late-period record that matters most.
A second covers record, crooner songs this time; minor.
Spare guitar and voice with Duke Garwood; slow and smoky.
More synth-blues in the Blues Funeral style; fine.
Gothic rock with Rob Marshall; solid but familiar.
Leans into 1980s synth-pop; a curiosity.
Written alongside his memoir Sing Backwards and Weep; the songs fill in the book.

about: Only five albums before Mark Sandman died on stage in 1999, so the path covers almost all of it.

records.n: The debut, already fully formed; it's on the list on its own too.
Two-string slide bass, baritone sax and drums, with Sandman murmuring about bars and bad decisions; the clearest statement of the sound.
Faster and funnier, with more spoken-word bits; a confident follow-up.
A major-label record, slower and more drowsy; the noir thickens.
Outtakes and live tracks; good, not essential.
Finished before Sandman's death and released after it; strings and organ around a darker, more spacious band.
Two discs of unreleased material; for after the albums.

about: Thirty-plus years of the same deep, deadpan voice; start with the Smog record that opened up, then follow it into the Bill Callahan albums.

records.n: Home-taped lo-fi noise and fragments; for completists.
Still lo-fi and lurching; songs starting to show through.
The first Smog album that sounds like songs; spiky and odd.
Abrasive, funny and sad by turns; an early cult favorite.
Bleak, slow and bare, his most depressive record; for later.
Pedal steel and French horn around quiet songs; the gentle prelude to Knock Knock.
A children's choir and Jim O'Rourke's production around songs about running away; Smog at its warmest.
Darker and more loose; good, overshadowed by its neighbors.
Rigid, repetitive grooves; the hardest Smog record to love.
Relaxed, country-tinged band record; minor.

records.t: A River Ain't Too Much to Love
records.n: Spare acoustic arrangements and plain, steady songs; the last Smog record and the first that sounds like Bill Callahan.
The first under his own name, gospel-tinged and sunny; transitional.

records.t: Sometimes I Wish We Were an Eagle
records.n: Strings and big open spaces, songs about God and eagles and hesitation; his best-loved record.

records.t: Rough Travel for a Rare Thing
records.n: Live in Melbourne, 2007; fine but not essential.
Seven long songs about America, history and himself, with a loose, jazzy band.
Flute, hand drums and patient songs about a man in a hotel bar; the calmest of the late records.
A dub remix of Dream River; a curiosity.
Twenty songs about marriage and fatherhood after a long silence; funny and tender.
Short story-songs that open with the line "Hello, I'm Johnny Cash"; good after the path.
Covers with Bonnie "Prince" Billy and many guests; a loose side project.
Looser and more jammy, with a full band; for later.
Live in Chicago with his touring band; a minor live record.
The newest record; hear it after the path.

about: David Berman's band, read like a book of poems: start at the warm middle, then follow him to the end, Purple Mountains.

records.n: Early lo-fi EP of tape noise and half-songs; for completists.
The first full album, still half a Pavement side project. Hear it last to see where the voice came from.
Back to the start: the first record built around Berman alone, after Malkmus and Bob Nastanovich were busy with Pavement. Shambling and wry.
The door. Stephen Malkmus is back on guitar, and Berman's lines ("In 1984 I was hospitalized for approaching perfection") land like short poems over loose country rock.
Recorded in Nashville, slower and more country, with pedal steel and Cassie Berman singing along. The sad, funny voice of the door with the edges sanded down.
A short EP from the Bright Flight period; the album already holds its best idea.
The comeback after addiction and a suicide attempt: the loudest, most rattled Silver Jews record, with Malkmus and Cassie both on it.
The final Silver Jews album: tidier and more upbeat, a little thinner than the run before it.
Collects the pre-album singles and EPs. Interesting as history, rough as listening.
His last record, made eleven years after he quit music and released weeks before he died. Plain, funny and unbearably direct about depression; it closes the study.

about: John Darnielle, songwriter and novelist: the Alpha couple's marriage falling apart, then his own childhood, then the band years.

records.n: Boombox-era Darnielle: one man, a guitar and a tape deck. The early records are a world of their own; save them for after the main path.
Another early boombox record; good songs buried in hiss.
Early tape-era record; for when the boombox sound has won you over.
The strongest of the pre-label tape records, but All Hail West Texas does that sound best.
Collected early cassette tracks; for completists.
More early tape tracks gathered on CD.
The last lo-fi album before the switch to 4AD; darker and quieter. A good first detour once the path is done.
The door. The first record with a real studio and a real label: a whole album about a married couple drinking themselves apart in a house in Florida.
Back to the boombox: fourteen songs recorded alone, tape hiss and all. "The Best Death Metal Band in Denton" is pure Darnielle.
The third early-rarities collection; the best of the three, still optional.
Meth addicts in a Portland apartment complex, drawn from his own years in Pomona. Bridges the Tallahassee sound and The Sunset Tree's honesty.
The autobiographical one, about growing up with an abusive stepfather. "This Year" is the shout-along; the rest is quieter and harder.
Hushed and lonely, close to whispered. Fine, but it repeats the mood of The Sunset Tree with less at stake.
Full band, strings, songs about cults and outsiders. Solid, a little even.

records.t: The Life of the World to Come
records.n: Twelve songs each named for a Bible verse, written as portraits rather than sermons. Quiet piano and guitar.
A loose set of songs with different producers; no strong center.
Horn arrangements by Owen Pallett and songs about people barely holding on. Good, but not essential.
A whole album about 1970s and 1980s territory wrestling, the heroes of his childhood. Proves the concept-record mode works outside his own life.
No guitars, Rhodes piano and horns, songs about aging goth musicians. Gentle and funny, a late-career peak.
A half-finished rock opera about a wizard, plus a song about Waylon Jennings. Fun, loose.
Recorded alone on a boombox during the 2020 lockdown, a deliberate return to the tape sound.
Recorded at Sam Phillips Recording in Memphis; warm and band-driven.
Recorded at Muscle Shoals; songs about disaster and survival.
Darnielle's action-movie record: guitars up, plots borrowed from 1970s revenge films.
A rock opera returning to Jenny, the biker girl from the All Hail West Texas era songs.

records.t: Through This Fire Across from Peter Balkan
records.n: A recent record; late-period, for after the path.

about: A tiny catalog: one strange masterpiece, the record that led to it, and the scraps Jeff Mangum left behind.

records.n: The first single and EP on Cher Doll; early sketches.
The first album, mostly Mangum alone with Robert Schneider producing. Rougher and noisier, with the same melodies trying to get out.

records.t: In the Aeroplane Over the Sea
records.n: The door. Fuzz guitar, singing saw, horns and Jeff Mangum's strained voice; Anne Frank's diary as a fever dream.
A solo Mangum show at an Athens coffee shop, released by him. Lovely, but the studio versions come first.
Old songs released with the vinyl box set, solo acoustic and close to the Aeroplane material. A small coda.

about: The first three records are a set: grief and family, then fear and religion, then where you grew up.

records.n: The early self-released EP; the songs are good but the band is not yet itself.
The door. Written in a season when several band members lost family; strings, accordion and big shouted choruses about kids, snow and the neighborhood.
Recorded in a church they bought outside Montreal, with a pipe organ. Darker, about media, war and fear.
A long record about growing up in Houston suburbs, sprawl and nostalgia. Closes the first-three-albums arc.
Produced with James Murphy, disco and Haitian rhythm, Orpheus and Eurydice and Kierkegaard's The Present Age. A real change of sound; the last essential one.
A satire of consumer culture that ends up sounding like the thing it mocks. Can wait.
A tighter, more earnest record, released just before abuse allegations against Win Butler. Optional.
Late-period record produced with Daniel Lanois; for after the main path.

records.t: Open Your Heart or Die Trying
records.n: The newest record; leave it until the first four have settled.

about: I know the middle two. The rest of the study is the debut, the farewell show, and the reunion record.

records.n: The debut, with a second disc of early singles like "Losing My Edge" and "Yeah". Jokier and rawer: James Murphy the record-collector DJ before he became the songwriter.
A 45-minute piece commissioned by Nike as a running soundtrack. Interesting, but it reads like a side commission.
Remixes and B-sides; skip unless you want more of the debut era.
The door, and the one I know. "All My Friends" and "Someone Great" are dance music about getting older and losing people.
The one I know second, meant as the last album. Longer songs, Bowie and Eno all through it.
Live-in-studio versions of songs you will already know by now.

records.t: The Long Goodbye: LCD Soundsystem Live at Madison Square Garden
records.n: The nearly four-hour farewell show from April 2011. Hear the songs the way the band played them, as the end of a story.
The reunion record: darker, slower, about death and aging, with Bowie's passing in the background. The real epilogue.
Studio-live set with a few covers; for fans.

about: Five albums over twenty-five years, each one stranger and freer than the last; start in the middle and work outward.

records.n: The debut at 18, with "Criminal". Glossier 1990s production than the rest; hear it last to see where she started.
The full title is a 90-word poem. Jon Brion produces again; jazzier and angrier than the debut, with tight, punchy piano songs.
The door. Jon Brion's arrangements, then a second producer after the label stalled it. Witty, theatrical songs about getting over people.
Stripped down to piano, voice and odd percussion. Raw, rhythmic and funny about her own mind.
Recorded mostly at home, banging on pots and furniture, with dogs barking. About getting free of everyone who held her down; the end of the path.

about: Four albums, each longer and denser than the last. Start with the big orchestral one, then go wide and back to the beginning.

records.n: Self-released early demos; the songs reappear in better form on the debut.
More early self-released demos.
The debut: just harp and that high, cracked voice. Hear it last, once the voice no longer surprises you.
The door. Five songs, 55 minutes, harp, a Van Dyke Parks orchestra, Steve Albini recording, lyrics like Victorian poetry.

records.t: Joanna Newsom and the Ys Street Band
records.n: Three songs played with a small touring band, including a new one. A footnote to Ys.
Three discs, two hours, looser and warmer, with piano and a band. Takes time, and rewards it.
An album about time looping back on itself, each song a separate arrangement. The most finished of the four.

about: Slowcore from Duluth: the hushed harmonies first, then the louder years, then the noise of the last records.

records.n: The debut: barely moving, almost no drums. Where the slowcore label came from.
Second album, more of the debut's stillness.
Longer songs, some drones; good but covered by the steps.
First album with Albini; spare and beautiful, the bridge to the door.
A short Christmas EP that became a cult favorite. Seasonal.

records.t: Things We Lost in the Fire
records.n: The door. Steve Albini recording, Mimi Parker and Alan Sparhawk singing in close harmony, very slow and very quiet.
Darker and murkier follow-up to the door.

records.t: A Lifetime of Temporary Relief: 10 Years of B-Sides and Rarities
records.n: Box set of B-sides and rarities; for completists.
Dave Fridmann produces, the guitars get loud, and the songs speed up a little. Same voices, more violence.
Sparse and angry about the Iraq war. Interesting, not essential.
Warm and pretty, a step back toward the early sound.
Produced by Jeff Tweedy; gentle and plain.
The first record with BJ Burton, pointing toward Double Negative.
Songs buried under digital distortion and static, like a radio dying. A late reinvention that sounds like 2018 felt.
The last album before Mimi Parker died in 2022. Harmonies fighting through the noise of Double Negative; it closes the study.

about: Montreal's anonymous collective: long instrumental pieces built from field recordings, strings and slow-building guitars.

records.n: The first album: darker and more broken, opening with a voice describing a dying city. Apocalypse as a tape collage.

records.t: Slow Riot for New Zerø Kanada
records.n: Two pieces; one samples a street preacher reading his own apocalyptic poem. The bridge between the first two albums.

records.t: Lift Your Skinny Fists Like Antennas to Heaven
records.n: The door. Four twenty-minute pieces, field recordings of a man on Coney Island, strings and guitars building to huge peaks.
Recorded with Steve Albini, angrier and more political, about war and arms companies. The last record before a ten-year break.
The comeback: two long, heavy pieces they had played live for years. Louder than anything before it.
One long piece in parts; drone-heavy and good, but repeats the comeback.
Warmer and more hopeful; for after the path.
A strong late record written in the pandemic; worth it once the path is done.

records.t: No Title as of 13 February 2024 28,340 Dead
records.n: Named for the Gaza death toll on the day it was finished. Late-period, for after the path.

about: Michael Gira's band in two lives: the brutal 1980s and 1990s, and the long, ecstatic reunion records. Start with the reunion.

records.n: The debut: slow, pounding no-wave noise, as bleak as music gets. Hear it once the later records make sense.
More of Filth's slow brutality.
Sound starts to open up toward Holy Money.
Jarboe arrives; the turn toward Children of God begins here.
Where the early brutality turns toward beauty: Jarboe's voice, religious imagery, acoustic passages next to the slow pounding.
A major-label record produced by Bill Laswell; Gira later disowned it.

records.t: White Light from the Mouth of Infinity
records.n: Lush and gothic, with acoustic guitars. A good detour after the path.
Close companion to White Light; can wait.
The most song-based 1990s record, with Gira and Jarboe writing almost pop-length pieces. A good way into that decade.
Meant as the last Swans record: two and a half hours of drones, tape collage and songs. The bridge to the reunion sound.
Live recordings from the 1995 and 1997 tours, the farewell before the long break.

records.t: My Father Will Guide Me up a Rope to the Sky
records.n: The reunion's first record, shorter and folkier than what came next.
The door. Two hours of repetition building to huge crescendos, with Karen O and Jarboe guesting. Hypnotic rather than punishing.
The Seer's follow-up, groovier and more physical. Long songs that lock into a riff and refuse to let go.
The last of the reunion trilogy with The Seer and To Be Kind; long and meditative.
A new lineup with guests; quieter and folkier.
Late-period, long and gentle.
Gira's last record with the current band setup; for after the path.

about: The road from synth-pop to silence: the two late albums first, Mark Hollis's solo coda, then back to see how the band got there.

records.n: The debut, in the shadow of Duran Duran. Only for the history.
Synth-pop with something odd underneath. Shows how far the band traveled.
Step back to see the turn: still songs, but with organ, choir and real instruments. "Life's What You Make It" was a hit.
The door. Improvised over months in a dark studio, then edited down: long quiet passages, sudden noise, organ, harmonica. A direct ancestor of Kid A.

records.t: Natural History: The Very Best of Talk Talk
records.n: Hits compilation; the studio albums do this better.
Even sparser, on Verve. Six pieces of near-silence and slow builds; the start of what people later called post-rock.
Hollis's only solo record, then he left music. Acoustic, chamber-jazz, almost whispered.
B-sides and remixes; for completists.
Live recording from The Colour of Spring tour.
Leftover tracks, including a few late-era pieces worth hearing after Laughing Stock.
Portishead's Beth Gibbons with Talk Talk bassist Paul Webb; smoky folk-jazz. A side road.

about: Cologne's Krautrock band: Stockhausen students and a Japanese street singer, playing long, locked grooves edited from hours of tape.

records.n: The first album, with American singer Malcolm Mooney. Rawer, closer to the Velvet Underground; "Yoo Doo Right" runs twenty minutes.
Film music, with both Mooney and Suzuki; "Mother Sky" is essential.
The door. A double album, Damo Suzuki singing, Jaki Liebezeit's drums locked in a loop, the second half turning into tape experiments. Radiohead covered and copied them.
Shorter, funkier and catchier: "Vitamin C" and "Spoon". The easiest Can to love.
Suzuki's last album: soft, floating, almost ambient. The side-long "Bel Air" is the end of their best run.
The first album after Suzuki left: instrumental, smooth and spacey. The last essential record.
Cleaner, more rock-oriented; good but less strange.
Includes the disco hit "I Want More"; the decline begins.
Outtakes and experiments from 1968 to 1975; the studio albums come first.
Ex-Traffic members join on percussion and bass; world-music grooves.
Generally considered their weakest; skip.
The last of the 1970s albums; for completists.
The shelved first album with Mooney, released later. Raw and worth hearing after Monster Movie.
A reunion with Mooney, recorded in 1986. A curiosity.
First of the archival live series; long improvisations. Optional.

about: Start with the Philips years, where she moved between jazz, blues, folk and protest without asking anyone's permission, then go back to the debut and forward to the furious live sets and the late exile records.

records.n: The debut, recorded in 1957: a classically trained pianist playing jazz trio standards, with Bach under the title track. Going back here shows where all of it started.
Her Colpix debut, arranged and orchestrated; the trio records show her better.
Early concert record, part live and part studio; fine, but the later live sets go further.
A good festival set from the early trio; worth it after the main path.
Colpix-era studio album of standards and blues; pleasant, not essential.
Strong club recording with "House of the Rising Sun"; for after the path.
An Ellington songbook with choir; more polished than the records on the path.
Her first Carnegie Hall record, mostly ballads; the 1964 concert is the one that matters.
Live at Carnegie Hall with "Mississippi Goddam," her answer to Medgar Evers and Birmingham. The point where the protest singer arrives.
Folk songs from the Village Gate shows; a minor Colpix release.
The first Philips album, with the original "Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood"; uneven around it.
Spare and heavy, ending in the ten-minute "Sinnerman," which builds like a revival meeting coming apart.

records.t: I Put a Spell on You
records.n: Her Philips sound with strings: the title song, "Feeling Good" and "Ne me quitte pas."
The door: the title track, "Four Women" and "Lilac Wine" all in one place. Dark, intimate and impossible to file under one genre.
Philips leftovers and live cuts; good songs, less shape than Wild Is the Wind.
Her first RCA record, a tight blues band and the bawdy "I Want a Little Sugar in My Bowl" next to "Backlash Blues," with words by Langston Hughes.
Big-band and orchestral pop arrangements; the most dated of the Philips run.
RCA album with "I Wish I Knew How It Would Feel to Be Free"; the rest is slicker.
Mostly live, recorded days after King's murder, with "Why? (The King of Love Is Dead)"; strong but rough.
Just her and the piano; lovely, quiet, for later.
Covers of Dylan, Cohen and the Bee Gees; interesting picks, uneven performances.
A live set that holds the first "To Be Young, Gifted and Black" and a long, loose "Who Knows Where the Time Goes."
More pop covers with strings; "My Way" is the reason to hear it.
Long, gospel-driven live and studio versions of George Harrison songs; for when you're already deep in.
The last RCA record, live and ragged, as she left America; a coda to the coda.
