The comeback after years away, cut in Brussels: reggae-tinged, weary and graceful. A good last stop.
Made in exile in Europe, personal and odd; worth hearing after Baltimore.
Her last studio album, ballads with strings; a farewell, not a starting point.

about: The three albums named in the row trace the arc from protest to sex to divorce; after that, the side roads show how strange and personal he got once Motown stopped steering.

records.t: The Soulful Moods of Marvin Gaye
records.n: His debut as a jazz crooner; he wanted to be Nat King Cole, and it shows.
Early Motown R&B with "Hitch Hike" and "Pride and Joy"; the singles do the job.
Another standards album; minor.
Show tunes; minor.

records.t: How Sweet It Is to Be Loved by You
records.n: Singles-era Motown built around the title hit; a compilation covers it.

records.t: A Tribute to the Great Nat King Cole
records.n: A tribute record to his idol; minor.
Mid-60s Motown with "Ain't That Peculiar"; the hits are on any best-of.
With Tammi Terrell: "Ain't No Mountain High Enough" and "Your Precious Love." Go back here last to hear the Motown hit machine at its best.
Home of "I Heard It Through the Grapevine"; the song matters more than the album.
Second Tammi Terrell album; good, but United covers the partnership.
Late-60s Motown with "Too Busy Thinking About My Baby"; minor.
The last duet album with Terrell, made as she was dying, partly with Valerie Simpson singing her parts.
The last album before What's Going On, mostly covers; minor.
The door: a song cycle about war, poverty and the planet, with the songs flowing into each other like a suite.
His film score: mostly instrumental, moody jazz-funk, and the title song.
The turn inward: sex and devotion, but with the same layered, jazzy production.
Duets with Diana Ross; a commercial pairing.
His return to the stage, with a long "Distant Lover"; for after the path.
Leon Ware's songs, Gaye's stacked vocals; a hazy, continuous mood record.
Double live set plus the studio track "Got to Give It Up"; for completists.
A double album about his divorce, with the royalties owed to his ex-wife. Bitter, funny, unpolished and the opposite of slick.
Made in exile in Europe and released against his wishes; paranoid, spiritual and unfinished in a good way.
"Sexual Healing" and drum machines; the most commercial record here.
A shelved 1972 album, released posthumously; interesting as the missing link after What's Going On.

about: The run from Music of My Mind to Songs in the Key of Life is five records in five years where he wrote, sang, played and programmed nearly everything; this path walks that run, then looks at the strange coda.

records.t: The Jazz Soul of Little Stevie
records.n: An instrumental debut at eleven; a curiosity.
Ray Charles covers by a child; a curiosity.

records.t: With a Song in My Heart
records.n: Standards; minor.

records.t: Recorded Live: The 12 Year Old Genius
records.n: Home of "Fingertips"; the single version is the story.
A beach-movie cash-in; minor.
Mid-60s Motown with "Uptight" and "Blowin' in the Wind"; the singles are enough.
Singles-era Motown; minor.

records.t: I Was Made to Love Her
records.n: The title hit is the reason; minor as an album.
A Christmas album.
An instrumental album under his name spelled backward; a curiosity.
Strong singles, a Motown album around them.
Hit-driven; minor.
The title hit and good covers; the last record before he took control.
His first self-written album, made just before he turned 21; a sketch of what came next.
"Superstition" and "You Are the Sunshine of My Life" on the same record; the moment he took full control.
The first fully self-produced record, made with the synth programmers Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff; rougher and more experimental than what follows.
The door: "Living for the City" and "Higher Ground," with him playing nearly every instrument. Social realism over synthesizers.
The quieter, more brooding sibling of Innervisions, with "You Haven't Done Nothin'" aimed at Nixon.

records.t: Songs in the Key of Life
records.n: A double album plus EP: jazz, funk, gospel, ballads and "Pastime Paradise." Sprawling on purpose.

records.t: Stevie Wonder's Journey Through "The Secret Life of Plants"
records.n: A mostly instrumental score for a documentary about plants. Baffling to buyers in 1979; strange and lovely now.
The last great one, with "Master Blaster" and "Happy Birthday," his campaign for a holiday for King.
Soundtrack with "I Just Called to Say I Love You"; skip.
Mid-80s gloss with "Part-Time Lover"; can wait.
Late-80s production; minor.
His songs for the Spike Lee film; for completists.
A long, warm late album; minor.
His most recent album; minor.

about: Curtis Mayfield's solo records of the early 70s brought long grooves, strings and wah guitar together with clear-eyed songs about the street; the path covers that peak, then goes back to the Impressions, where the civil rights songs started.

records.n: The Impressions' early civil rights statement; the title song is the one to know.
The title song is one of the great American songs; the album around it is slighter.
The Impressions on his own Curtom label, with the title song and "Choice of Colors." The civil rights songs before the solo career.
Late Impressions with "Choice of Colors" carried over from the singles; for after the path.
The door: "Move On Up" and "(Don't Worry) If There's a Hell Below, We're All Going to Go." Psychedelic soul with horns, strings and a conscience.
The Impressions after he left the lineup; he still wrote and produced it.
The second solo record, longer and looser, with "We People Who Are Darker Than Blue."
Recorded at the Bitter End in Greenwich Village with a small band; his guitar and falsetto up close.
A soundtrack that outlasted the film: "Pusherman" and "Freddie's Dead" tell the story the movie glamorizes.
About soldiers coming home from Vietnam to a broken country; lush and angry.
Solid mid-70s groove; the peak records say more.
Short, mellow follow-up; minor.
His songs for the film, sung by Gladys Knight & the Pips.

records.t: There's No Place Like America Today
records.n: Slow, stripped back and bleak; the cover is a breadline under a billboard of a smiling white family.
His songs for the film, sung by the Staple Singers; the title song was a hit.
Drifting toward disco; minor.
His songs for the film, sung by Aretha Franklin.
Soft and romantic; minor.
A score for a prison film; for completists.
A disco record; skip.
Late-70s gloss; minor.
Minor.
Minor.
A modest return to form; still minor.

records.t: We Come in Peace with a Message of Love
records.n: Minor.
His last album before the stage accident that paralyzed him; minor.
Recorded lying down, a line at a time, after the accident; moving to hear, but not the place to start.

about: The songs came out as singles, so start with the hits and then hear the records built around them, including the dark recitations he cut as Luke the Drifter.

records.n: His first 10-inch LP; the songs are on the hits set.
One of only two LPs out in his lifetime: eight blues-leaning sides, "Lovesick Blues" among them.

records.t: Hank Williams as Luke the Drifter
records.n: Recitations and moral sermons under a pseudonym; gloomy, strange and the closest he came to a short story.
The first posthumous collection; superseded by later compilations.
His gospel songs; the other half of the honky-tonk story.
Posthumous LP of honky-tonk sides; covered by the hits.
Another posthumous gathering, with the title song; for after the path.
The door: the singles in one place, "I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry" to "Your Cheatin' Heart." Short, plain songs that hit hard.
Ten discs, demos and radio shows included; for when one album isn't enough.

about: Daniel Romano went from rhinestone heartbreak country to wordy psych rock and then to a band that records nearly everything live. Start with the record where he turned, go back to the country years, then follow him forward.

records.n: Rustic folk with Frederick Squire and Julie Doiron, mostly public-domain songs.
An early EP of folk ballads.
The solo debut, folk turning toward country; the sound gets sharper on the next records.
Downcast retro country; Come Cry With Me does the same thing better.
Straight heartbreak country in a Nudie suit; the revivalist at his purest.

records.t: If I've Only One Time Askin'
records.n: Countrypolitan strings and steel, sadder and more ornate than the one before.
The break: country colliding with 60s pop, rock and Leonard Cohen talk-singing.
His punk band; loud and short, a side road.
The door: his Dylan-in-1966 record, wordy, warped and funny. The country singer gone strange.
Folky, psychedelic and lyrically knotty; he says it came to him while driving through the Prairies.
A surprise Bandcamp release of quiet country-folk; for after the path.
Released with Human Touch: 70s-style pop rock with a few fuzzed-out turns.
More punk from Ancient Shapes.
Ancient Shapes again; for punk days.

records.t: How Ill Thy World Is Ordered
records.n: The best of the 2020 flood: the Outfit full-band, horn-laden and euphoric.
A full turn back to classic country with the Outfit, male and female harmonies and slide guitar.
The first of the 2020 releases, made alone in quarantine: sax, baroque pop and psychedelia.
Six angry, playful power-pop songs with members of Fucked Up and Jade Hairpins.
The Outfit live in Scandinavia in 2019, mostly Modern Pressure and Finally Free songs rocked up.
Soft, sunny psych pop recorded alone in about a week.
A single 22-minute prog piece with Tool's Danny Carey on drums; a curiosity.

records.t: Daniel Romano's Outfit Do (What Could Have Been) Infidels by Bob Dylan & the Plugz
records.n: Dylan's Infidels re-imagined as if he'd made it with the L.A. punk band the Plugz; a fun experiment.
Raw hardcore with Steve Lambke of the Constantines, as the band Spider Bite.
British-style psych folk with Kelly Sloan and David Nardi as Alias Ensemble.
The tenth 2020 release, solo and Beatles-breezy; a compact sampler of the year.
With the Outfit, his live band, at their own studio on the Welland Canal: electric, horn-heavy rock, power pop and psychedelia.
Twelve songs with him playing nearly everything; for after the path.
A live Outfit record; the studio albums come first.
One song in twelve parts, about 33 minutes, with the Outfit; ambitious, but not where to start.
The second Spider Bite record.
Tight garage rock with MC5 and Stooges energy; strong, and a good next step after the path.
A recent live record.
The newest, credited to Outfit, with songwriting shared across the band; recorded live to tape.

about: Start with the dust storms, then the plain-spoken Asch recordings and the long conversation with Alan Lomax, and end with Billy Bragg and Wilco setting his unrecorded lyrics to music.

records.n: The door: songs of the Okie migration, "Tom Joad" retelling The Grapes of Wrath in seventeen verses.
Children's songs; charming but minor.

records.t: Songs to Grow on for Mother and Child
records.n: More children's songs; minor.
Songs with readings from his autobiography; a decent sampler.
A song cycle on the executed anarchists, commissioned by Moe Asch in 1946.
Recorded with Alan Lomax in 1940: songs, stories and talk. You hear the man, not just the songbook.
Labor songs, including "Ludlow Massacre" and "1913 Massacre"; the angriest set.
Songs written for the Bonneville Power Administration in 1941, "Roll On, Columbia" among them.

records.t: This Land Is Your Land: The Asch Recordings, Vol. 1
records.n: The 1940s Asch sessions, with the full "This Land Is Your Land," the verses about private property included.

records.t: Muleskinner Blues: The Asch Recordings, Vol. 2
records.n: More of the Asch sessions; after Vol. 1.
His unrecorded lyrics set to music by Billy Bragg and Wilco; a bridge to the Wilco path.

records.t: Hard Travelin': The Asch Recordings, Vol. 3
records.n: More of the Asch sessions.

records.t: Buffalo Skinners: The Asch Recordings, Vol. 4
records.n: More of the Asch sessions.

about: There are only twenty-nine songs, so one set holds all of it; the other records here are the LPs that carried the myth to Dylan, Clapton and the Stones.

records.t: King of the Delta Blues Singers
records.n: The LP that Dylan and Keith Richards heard; same songs, now inside the complete set.

records.t: King of the Delta Blues Singers, Vol. II
records.n: The rest of the songs; also inside the complete set.
The door and the whole catalog: every side from the 1936 and 1937 sessions plus alternate takes. Spare, fast guitar and a high, haunted voice.
A newer remaster of everything; pick one complete set, not both.

about: Two Chess albums of singles hold most of what matters; after them come the folk-blues repackagings, the odd psychedelic record he hated, and the last studio album.

records.n: The door: "Smokestack Lightning" and "How Many More Years." A huge, rasping voice over Hubert Sumlin's jagged guitar.
The rocking chair album: "Spoonful," "Back Door Man," "Little Red Rooster," all Willie Dixon songs, all covered later by the rock bands.
Crown budget LP of early Memphis sides; the same period is better covered elsewhere.
More Chess singles, sold to the folk-revival crowd; "Killing Floor" is here.
Earlier 1950s sides; rougher and older-sounding.
A jam with Muddy Waters and Bo Diddley; fun, loose, minor.
Chess's attempt at psychedelic blues; the cover says he didn't like it. Fuzz and wah over the old songs; strange and worth hearing once.
A funk-leaning studio record; minor.
With Clapton, Winwood, Wyman and Watts; famous, but the British players are too polite.
Live at Silvio's in Chicago; for after the path.
A Chess double compilation of the singles; superseded.
His last studio album, recorded when he was ill; tough and unshowy.
A posthumous-era odds-and-ends compilation.
Three discs; when one album isn't enough.
A single-disc hits set if you want the singles without the original LPs.

about: Skip James made two careers thirty-five years apart: the 1931 Paramount sides and the 1960s rediscovery records. Start with the later one, where the sound is clear, then go back.

records.t: Greatest of the Delta Blues Singers
records.n: His first rediscovery LP; the Vanguard records sound better.
The door: "Hard Time Killin' Floor Blues" and "Cypress Grove" recorded in good sound, his falsetto and minor-key guitar intact.
The second Vanguard album; quieter and just as eerie.
A Vanguard compilation of the 60s material; superseded by the two albums.
The 1931 Paramount sides, scratchy and otherworldly: "Devil Got My Woman" and "I'm So Glad."
A 1964 session released decades later; for after the path.

about: Start with the record where the noise turned into pop songs, then walk back through the albums that built it, with Panda Bear's solo record in the middle where it belongs.

records.t: Spirit They're Gone, Spirit They've Vanished
records.n: Avey Tare and Panda Bear's lo-fi debut, credited at the time to the two of them. Interesting as a sketch; can wait.
Shrill, fractured experiments. For after the path, if ever.
The dark, droning, abrasive one. Hard going, but it shows how far out they started.
Recorded live on a porch in one take; a gentler preview of Sung Tongs.
Just Avey Tare and Panda Bear with acoustic guitars and campfire chants. Strange and tender, and the root of everything after.
Guitars drenched in reverb and detuned piano; a warm, woozy band record that sounds like summer heat.
A short, quiet meeting with the British folk singer. Nice, but minor.
The step just before the door, harsher and more electric, with Avey Tare's yelping on "For Reverend Green" and "Fireworks."
Sample loops and Beach Boys harmonies stacked into long sunlit songs. As important to the band's sound as any of their own albums.
Their clearest record: big sub-bass, layered harmonies and songs like "My Girls" that hold still long enough to sing along. If this clicks, the rest opens up.
Leftovers from the Merriweather era, including "What Would I Want? Sky." Worth hearing right after the door if it hooks you.
Crowded, loud and busy; the follow-up to their peak tries too hard.
Short, choppy pop songs. The weakest of the band records.
All four members back together, calmer and more patient, with songs built from live playing. A good late close to the path.
Long, live-sounding songs from the Time Skiffs lineup. Fine once the path is done.
